title: Going overseas: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and the US — go there first so you can get big
dek: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there in order to get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.
why: Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas-investing experience into four choices, each counterintuitive but backed by cases and numbers; the back half, on AI rebuilding organisations and pricing, is the densest.
who: Founders building or preparing overseas brands, cross-border e-commerce operators, and early-stage investors watching consumer going-global.
skip: The opening small talk and the 15th-anniversary congratulations, about 1 minute, can be skipped.

points.h: The old cross-border mega-seller playbook is dead
points.body: Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ model popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset — dozens or hundreds of accounts at a time; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and plenty of investors loved them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely you are to get traffic. When a platform's goods aren't plentiful enough, he doesn't object to distribution; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, there are three red lines: goods not matching the listing harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and slipping in little cards to build private-domain traffic harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel puts enormous weight on consumer experience, and these behaviours run straight into that wall.

points.h: Of the four choices, region comes first
points.body: Wei Zhe says it isn't just cross-border e-commerce — all of life is about choice mattering more than effort. He lays out four choices: region, channel, product category, brand positioning. On region he has always argued for seizing the European and American market first, because purchasing power is strong, internet penetration is high, and more importantly a brand can build momentum there. This isn't their invention — when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and America. On category they change their advice every three years: the first three years they backed products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification — Anker's power banks, for instance, were almost identical back then apart from voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and China-abroad commonality offered no differentiation; the most recent three years it's product 3.0 — electrified, chipped, algorithmic.

points.h: You don't go to Europe and the US after getting big — you go there to get big
points.body: Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and the US once I'm big’, and he says it's exactly backwards: you go to Europe and the US in order to get big. He cites the swimwear company Cupshe — a husband and wife, 50,000 dollars of inventory, and the first stop was the US. Fifty thousand dollars is sales inventory, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. Looking recently at AI smart hardware, they start from a thousand or ten thousand products on the Kickstarter crowdfunding platform, even taking prepayment before placing orders, with no capital — that too is a great way to test the water. He even advises big companies entering the European and American market to learn from small startups. They always say the needle has to be fine enough to pierce through, and big or small, companies should first nail the four singles: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

points.h: After AI, good companies don't just find demand — they create it
points.body: Wei Zhe says that with AI, excellent companies shouldn't go looking for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He cites a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: it used to be unpowered, and they electrified it, adding a chip and an algorithm — the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, since the movements of the sky follow rules. He wasn't an astronomy hobbyist before but he'd buy one: at home in Silicon Valley you tap once, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you three in the morning is the best time, you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it has shot it for you. That lets anyone become a very good astronomy hobbyist. Another example: a cross-border class student doing curtains, which didn't sell well in the US once electrified because American electricians are expensive, so he put a solar panel on the window and turned electric curtains that needed an electrician into something you can DIY; the business went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

points.h: In the AI era, still charging subscriptions means you're behind
points.body: Wei Zhe says that in the AI era, still thinking in terms of subscription fees means you're behind again; they're all urging companies toward back-end charging, software charging — what they call tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest approach, a bit like advertising that used to charge by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks of vacation this month, isn't a monthly subscription wasting two weeks? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not go back to the old SaaS model of 9.99 dollars a month. One AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and charges nothing if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers — you top up, then one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

Wei Zhe has a formulation: AI-plus or plus-AI. He flips the phrase around — what he favours more is plus-AI, not today's AI-plus. The difference: plus-AI takes hardware humans have already accepted and makes it AI; AI-plus creates hardware never seen before because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept entirely new hardware. Oura makes a ring, for instance, because you already accepted rings; something that hangs a camera under your neck is harder for me — I've never accepted that hardware. So they're very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. One capacitive stylus they invested in is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad; it doesn't add another pen, it just makes your pen AI. He also particularly wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness-equipment companies, replacing the fitness instructor on the screen with an AI-generated one — you want a man, it's a man; you want a Black instructor, it's a Black instructor; install two cameras and it can coach your workout with AI.

points.h: Channels aren't flat — they're a pyramid
points.body: Wei Zhe says channels aren't about more channels meaning more roads, with each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and rules about which channel a new product launches in first. What counts as a light-goods channel, what counts as the main waist channel for volume — the pyramid design differs by category and by brand. He cites Anker: making power-bank mecha gear seems a bit low, so to enter the consumer-electronics high ground with Soundcore headphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it actually sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can transform the brand — Apple is the tip of the pyramid. Pop Mart has to open on London's Oxford Street; even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it has to hold that position. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel — when Amazon delists you, you dump it there; you can't sell on Amazon and there too, consumers get confused.

points.h: R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0
points.body: Wei Zhe says he really dislikes throwing money at marketing. Many Chinese brands going overseas, or cross-border e-commerce companies, are happy to add 2% of revenue as marketing spend, but consumers don't get it. He asks: do you dare add 2% of revenue as R&D spend? He has met many bosses at the one or two billion scale; at one billion they say 20 million for R&D, and I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem — you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing spend makes the platform happy and consumers get nothing; but 2% thrown into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed a good product speaks for itself, and marketing is just — your R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0; if your thing is good you can amplify it, but if you don't have that 1, never put on a lot of 0s. He gives three signals to judge by: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and crush it with double the performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online and it pushes offline channels to come find you.

points.h: AI doesn't just change products — it rebuilds every role
points.body: Wei Zhe says two things about AI matter greatly for companies, and big, medium and small companies all need to do them well: first, combining products with AI; second, how the organisation changes through AI. He sees cross-border e-commerce companies as, of all the industries he has encountered, the one that most should use AI to transform every single role. Every role should ask what AI can do for it: product selection, content generation, ad-placement choices — all essentially algorithms; it used to rely on human experience, and experience is certainly no match for algorithmic iteration. Customer service becomes AI — there is no customer service anymore, customer service is just you training your customer-service agent; for ad placement you train an agent; product selection, product display, product image and video generation all become AI. He says this is the first and only industry he has seen where the entire company's organisational chain can be transformed by AI. He also says what they oppose most is putting lots of people overseas — with or without AI they oppose it; they call it: no unnecessary people overseas.

points.h: Don't just let AI do the work — let it into the decisions
points.body: Wei Zhe puts AI and organisation very simply: many companies have a P series and an M series — P is professional, M is management. Many people are used to letting AI do P work, doing the job; generating images was originally P-series work. But truly formidable companies don't just let AI do P-series work — they gradually let it do the work of a Manager, Director or VP. He gives a real AI pricing case: the company wanted to sell at 35 euros, AI said you can sell at 55, the company really went to 55 and it really sold, with volume about the same as at 35, but 20 euros more profit. He says AI has no courage — it's bolder than you, it has compared everything across the whole web for you. He also says that even if AI hallucinates, with so many large models across China and the US, they won't all dream the same dream at once, so you must cross-validate.
